    // # The IMesh2D obligations
    //
    // Faces index the same points the caller passed in, so a triangulation can be
    // traced back to the ring it came from.

    // The polygon triangulated over its own vertices, by ear clipping.
    Triangulate(p: Polygon2D): TriangleMesh2D
        => (p.Points, p.Points.TriangulateRings(0.Range));

    // The convex polygon triangulated over its own vertices. Convexity makes every
    // corner an ear, so the fan from the first vertex is already a triangulation
    // and no clipping pass is needed.
    Triangulate(p: ConvexPolygon2D): TriangleMesh2D
        => (p.Points, (p.Points.Count - 2).MapRange(i
            => TriangleFace(VertexIndex(0), VertexIndex(i + 1), VertexIndex(i + 2))));
```

    // The region triangulated over the pool of its boundary and hole vertices, by
    // ear clipping after every hole has been bridged into the boundary.
    Triangulate(r: PolygonWithHoles2D): TriangleMesh2D
        => (r.PointPool, r.PointPool.TriangulateRings(r.HoleStarts));
```

## Line 637

**Source:** [stdlib/geometry/triangulation.library.plato, line 637](../../../../../stdlib/geometry/triangulation.library.plato#L637).

```plato

    // The set triangulated over the concatenated pools of its components. An empty
    // set yields an empty mesh, which is the honest answer rather than a
    // precondition — Boolean operations produce empty results routinely.
    Triangulate(s: PolygonSet2D): TriangleMesh2D
        => (s.PointPool, s.Polygons.Count.Range.Reduce(TriangleFace.NoFaces, (faces, k)
            => faces.Concatenate(s.Polygons[k].Triangulate.Faces.ShiftedFaces(s.ComponentStart(k)))));
```
